title: Home tab: project dashboard (in-flight work, velocity, recent PRs)
body:
## Problem

The app opens into Queue, but there's no at-a-glance answer to "what is this project doing right now?" — what branches are in flight, how much work is moving through the pipeline, what shipped recently. You have to assemble that from Queue + Activity + GitHub.

## What to build

A **Home** section (first in the sidebar, default on launch) summarizing:

- **In flight** — running scouts and the running build, with branch names, elapsed time, and the task each serves (`/sessions`, `/builds`; builds carry `branch`, `base_branch`, `head_sha`, `pr_number`, and all three timestamps).
- **Recent PRs** — builds that succeeded, newest first: PR number linking out to GitHub, title/task, when. `pr_number` is an identifier only — open/merged/closed state is GitHub's; link out rather than showing state (see decisions below).
- **Velocity** — counts over a trailing window (e.g. 7 days) derived from the event log: tasks ingested, specs produced, specs approved, builds completed, PRs opened. Event kinds exist for each: `task_ingested`, `spec_created`, `spec_queue_status_changed`, `build_completed`, `pull_request_opened`.
- **Needs you** — specs awaiting review, failed builds; click through to Queue.

## Findings from scoping against the live API (verified, not guessed)

1. **Don't compute volume from `/tasks`** — it returns only live tasks (5 now) while the event log holds 32 `task_ingested` events; closed-upstream work is reconciled away, understating throughput ~6×. Volume must come from `/events`.
2. `/events` defaults to the newest 100 (full log already 163). A naive fetch silently loses history and renders a wrong chart. Page with `?since=`/`?limit=` from seq 1, or bound the window server-side.
3. `/builds` embeds full PR-body markdown plus every touched path (~9KB for two builds). A dashboard that polls it pulls prose it never renders. **The one server change this likely needs: a list projection dropping `summary`/`files_touched`** (keep the full shape on `/builds/{id}`).
4. `/spec-queue` populates only `spec_id`, `task_id`, `status` — `created_at` is null, so "3 specs awaiting review" works but "waiting since Tuesday" doesn't without joining `/specs`.
5. Task `updated_at` is bumped in bulk by the poller — useless as an activity signal. Use `ingested_at` and the event log for recency.
6. New wire shapes need fixtures: `fixtures/` (#763) fails compilation on unhandled variants, so any new endpoint/projection ships its fixture in the same pass. The Swift client's typed `Event`/`EventPayload` should feed the velocity section — don't re-parse SSE.

## Design decisions already made (do not revisit)

- **Never persist or mirror GitHub-owned PR state** (mergeable/merged/CI). Recent-PRs links out; if PR state ever becomes a display need, it's a query-at-render-time question, not a stored field. See CLAUDE.md sync rules.
- Velocity counters derive from the append-only event log at read time — no new counter state.

## Acceptance criteria

- Home section renders the four blocks above from live data, updating via the existing SSE-driven refresh.
- Velocity numbers match a hand count of the event log over the same window.
- Any new server projection ships with fixtures + Swift decoding tests in the same PR.

title: Transcript view is laggy on real scout runs
body:
## Problem

The session transcript pane gets very laggy during a live scout run (observed on #790's session). The causes are the same family just fixed in the Chat pane (PRs #792/#793), and `TranscriptView` has all of them:

- **Parsing inside `body`, per row, per frame:** `TranscriptRecord(line)` runs `JSONSerialization` + shape-matching in `TranscriptLineView.body`, and `LazyVStack` re-evaluates row bodies continuously while scrolling. Every scroll frame re-parses every visible stream-json record.
- **Whole-view re-evaluation per SSE line:** `follow()` does `lines.append(line)` on each arriving line, invalidating the `ForEach` while the scout streams (hundreds of lines) — combined with per-row parsing this compounds.
- **`.textSelection(.enabled)` on many small Texts** — each becomes its own AppKit selectable-text host (the exact mechanism that locked up Chat scrolling).
- **Unbounded raw walls** (see #795) — multi-KB single Texts make layout worse.

## What to build

Apply the Chat pane's fixes (see `app/Tasks/Markdown.swift` `MarkdownCache` and PR #793 for the pattern):

1. Parse each line once — either cache `TranscriptRecord` keyed by line identity (lines are immutable), or parse at append time in `follow()` and store the parsed projection in state instead of re-deriving in `body`.
2. Scope `.textSelection(.enabled)` to disclosure bodies (the copy-worthy expanded content), not every collapsed label/caption.
3. Reconsider the container: rows are cheap once parsing is cached and walls are collapsed (#795); if lag persists, the transcript is append-only so an equivalent of the Chat pane's non-lazy choice — or row height capping — applies.

## Acceptance criteria

- Scrolling a live, multi-hundred-line transcript is smooth while lines continue to stream in.
- No JSON parsing occurs during scroll (verifiable by profiling or a parse counter in debug).

title: Research: off-the-shelf agent components (prompts, tools, harness patterns)
body:
## Problem

We build a lot from first principles — scout/review/build prompts, review policy, agent tooling choices. Meanwhile the Claude Code orchestration space is moving fast and lots of teams are publishing prompts, skills, MCP servers, and harness patterns for exactly this shape of system. We haven't surveyed what can be pulled off the shelf.

## What to build

A written survey — deliverable is a report at `docs/research/off-the-shelf.md` (no code) — covering:

- **Claude Code / Agent SDK features we're not using**: skills, hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse for guardrails, PreCompact), subagents, MCP servers, structured outputs, `--append-system-prompt` patterns. For each: what it replaces in our roadmap, adoption cost.
- **Published prompt/skill libraries** relevant to scouting (issue → spec), code review, and PR authoring — including Anthropic's own published skills and cookbook material.
- **Open-source Claude Code orchestration layers** (queue managers, multi-agent runners, review bots). What they solved that we haven't hit yet; whether any component is directly reusable vs pattern-only.
- **Our own v1 salvage list** (CLAUDE.md notes v1's orchestrator review-policy prompt, diff-churn ranking, two-pass triage→deep-review) — compare against what's now standard off the shelf; recommend salvage vs replace.

Conclude with a ranked adopt/skip/watch list, each entry one paragraph: what, where it plugs in, cost.

## Constraints

- Recommendations must respect the load-bearing rules: Claude Code is the engine (no home-rolled loops), the Scout/Builder information barrier, no persisted GitHub-owned state, GitHub writes through the server only.
- This is a research task: the spec/report is the deliverable. No implementation in this issue — follow-up issues get filed per adopted item.

## Acceptance criteria

- `docs/research/off-the-shelf.md` exists with the four sections and the ranked list.
- Every "adopt" entry names the concrete integration point in this codebase (file/loop/prompt it would change).

title: Transcript view cleanup: raw JSON walls, repeated 'session started' rows
body:
## Problem

Dogfooding #790's scout run, the session transcript pane (`app/Tasks/TranscriptView.swift`) degrades badly on real output:

- **Raw stream-json walls.** Some records render as the raw JSON line — thousands of characters with visible `\n\t` escapes, uncollapsed, dominating the pane. The lenient parser (`TranscriptRecord.init`) falls through to `.raw` whenever a line fails `JSONSerialization` or doesn't match the expected shape, and `.raw` renders the entire line as flat monospaced text. Likely trigger: oversized records (a big `Read` tool_result) truncated by the transcript byte cap, so the JSON no longer parses. Whatever the cause, an unparseable line must degrade gracefully — collapsed by default with a short preview, never a full dump.
- **Repeated "session started" rows.** Every `"type":"system"` record maps to `.systemInit`, but Claude Code emits system records with multiple subtypes — a real run shows clusters of bare "session started" lines (only the first carries the model name). Match on `subtype == "init"` for the session-started row; render other system subtypes compactly or not at all.

## What to build

In `TranscriptLineView` / `TranscriptRecord`:

1. `.raw` renders as a `DisclosureGroup` (like tool results) when the line exceeds a modest length (~200 chars): label = first line truncated, body = full text, monospaced, selectable. Short raw lines can stay inline.
2. `system` records: `subtype == "init"` → session-started row as today; other subtypes → skip or a single-line secondary caption with the subtype.
3. Tool-result summaries and tool-use inputs get a length cap in the collapsed body too (e.g. first N KB with a "truncated" marker) — a 100KB file read shouldn't produce a 100KB Text even inside a disclosure.
4. If truncation by the server-side transcript byte cap is confirmed as the raw-JSON trigger, note it in the code; consider having the scout-supervisor or server mark truncated lines so the client can label them instead of failing to parse silently.

## Acceptance criteria

- A transcript containing an unparseable multi-KB line renders it collapsed with a one-line preview.
- A real scout run shows exactly one "session started" row per actual session init.
- Existing parsed renderings (assistant text, thinking, tool use/result, final result row) unchanged.

title: Test suite speed: adopt nextest and stop building binaries inside tests
body:
Follow-up to #799, which was closed as research. That research produced a full per-lever attribution of where the suite's wall clock goes; this issue is the subset worth building.

## Why only a subset

The premise of #799 — a workspace suite exceeding 10 minutes — was never reproduced. Measured at `cf8e32a`:

| | this Mac (M-series, warm) | scout's box (4-core aarch64 Linux) |
|---|---|---|
| full `cargo test --workspace` | 35.4s | ~12s execution, 25–26s edit→green |
| relink after `touch crates/tasks/src/lib.rs` | 2.35s | 7.2s |
| cold build, fresh `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` | 25.6s | 44s |

Neither machine is within an order of magnitude of 10 minutes, so the levers that target **link volume** are optimizing something that is ~6% of the loop on macOS. Those are deferred below until the reported condition is reproduced.

## In scope

1. **cargo-nextest**, with `.config/nextest.toml`. Per-test process isolation and real parallelism is where the win is on a suite that is almost entirely waiting on child processes. Include a `default` profile (slow-test warning, hard kill, leak timeout, `final-status-level = "slow"` so every run prints its slowest tests) and a `ci` profile (`fail-fast = false`, retries — nextest marks retried tests flaky rather than hiding them).
2. **Stop shelling out to `cargo build` inside tests.** `crates/{scout,builder}-supervisor/tests/integration.rs` exec their own package's binary, which cargo already builds and hands over as `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_<pkg>")`. Pure waste today.
3. **A `workspace_bin()` helper for the cross-package case.** The `tasks` suite execs the supervisors, which live in other packages, so `CARGO_BIN_EXE_` is unavailable. Prefer a `TASKS_TEST_BIN_DIR` env var, fall back to building, and memoize so a bare `cargo test` pays it once per binary rather than once per test.
4. **`make test` / `make test-cargo`.** `test` prebuilds the supervisors, exports `TASKS_TEST_BIN_DIR`, runs nextest, and fails with install instructions if nextest is absent. `test-cargo` is the `cargo test` path, which must stay fully supported for anyone who doesn't install nextest.
5. **Document the convention** in CLAUDE.md: tests exec binaries, they don't build them.

## Explicitly out of scope

Deferred until someone reproduces a genuinely slow suite, because on measured hardware they cost more in review and muscle memory than they buy:

- Merging `crates/tasks/tests/*.rs` into a single `tests/integration/` binary. Real on Linux (7.2s → ~1.2s relink combined with the other linker levers), ~nothing on macOS, and it changes how everyone filters tests (`cargo test --test run <filter>` becomes `--test integration run::<filter>`).
- `[profile.dev] debug = "line-tables-only"`.
- The LLD stanza in `.cargo/config.toml`.
- Retuning the scout timeout tests from 2s to 1s. Cuts margin on a box-specific measurement; floored anyway by `ScoutError::Timeout { secs: u64 }`.

## Notes

- **nextest does not run doctests.** This workspace has two (`vm-pool-client`), so `make test` must not be the only command CI runs — pair it with `cargo test --doc --workspace`, or use `make test-cargo`.
- Two tests legitimately report `LEAK`: deallocating a VM doesn't kill the agent under it, so the timeout tests leave a `sleep` holding an inherited pipe. Set the leak timeout to tolerate that without masking anything worse.
- cargo-nextest becomes a developer prerequisite for `make test` (`cargo install cargo-nextest --locked`). Plain `cargo test --workspace` must keep working.

## Open question, worth answering before the deferred items come back

Where was the 10 minutes observed? The leading hypothesis is that it was not compile or link time but a **stall** — vm-pool unreachable or wedged, letting the timeout-based tests run to their full deadlines. If that's it, the fix is failing fast when the socket is absent, and none of the build-mechanics levers are relevant.

title: RFC: Double Diamond Architecture - Serial Implementation Model
body:
## Problem Statement

The current model has N agents implementing N tasks in parallel. This leads to:
- **Endless conflicts** — N agents touching overlapping code
- **Duplicate work** — Agents discovering the same blockers, making similar decisions
- **No shared context** — Each agent starts fresh, doesn't know what others are doing

## Proposed Solution: Double Diamond Architecture

Transform the execution model from "parallel implementation with reactive conflict resolution" to "parallel exploration with serial implementation."

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           DIAMOND 1: EXPLORATION                             │
│                              (Parallel, Divergent)                           │
│                                                                              │
│   Issues ──► Scout Agents ──► Throwaway Implementation ──► Spec Artifact    │
│              (N parallel)      (discover pitfalls)         (markdown)        │
│                                                                              │
│   Output: Refined issue with implementation spec, known blockers,            │
│           edge cases discovered, dependencies identified                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         SPEC QUEUE (Convergent Point)                        │
│                                                                              │
│   Completed specs ranked and prioritized for implementation                  │
│   Orchestrator reviews specs, may request clarification or reject            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       DIAMOND 2: IMPLEMENTATION                              │
│                              (Serial, Focused)                               │
│                                                                              │
│   Spec ──► Builder Agent ──► Implementation ──► PR ──► Change Queue         │
│            (1 at a time)    (with full context)                              │
│                                                                              │
│   Input: Validated spec + context of in-flight/finished work                 │
│   Output: PR ready for merge                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           CHANGE QUEUE (Merge)                               │
│                              (Serial, Guarded)                               │
│                                                                              │
│   PRs ranked ──► CI/Checks ──► Conflict Resolution ──► Merge                │
│                                                                              │
│   If changes needed: route back to appropriate phase                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Key Insight

**Throwaway implementation forces real understanding.**

An agent that just reads an issue and writes a spec is guessing. An agent that actually implements the feature discovers the real pitfalls, edge cases, and dependencies. That implementation experience gets distilled into a Spec — then a second agent re-implements from that validated knowledge, serially, without conflicts.

---

## Terminology

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **Scout** | Agent in Diamond 1. Explores a problem through throwaway implementation. Produces a Spec. |
| **Spec** | The artifact from Diamond 1. Markdown containing implementation knowledge distilled from actual coding. |
| **Spec Queue** | Ordered list of completed Specs awaiting implementation. The convergent point. |
| **Builder** | Agent in Diamond 2. Implements from a Spec with full context. Produces a PR. |
| **Change Queue** | Ordered list of PRs awaiting merge. Handles CI, conflicts, final integration. |

---

## Diamond 1: Exploration Phase

### Scout Workflow

1. Claim issue from work queue
2. Create throwaway branch (`scout/<issue>-<uuid>`)
3. **IMPLEMENT THE FEATURE/FIX COMPLETELY**
   - Write the code
   - Fix lint errors
   - Make CI/checks pass
   - Handle edge cases discovered
4. Distill implementation into Spec artifact
5. Post Spec as structured comment on issue
6. Delete throwaway branch
7. Transition issue to "spec-ready" state

### Scout Success Criteria

The Scout's implementation must be **complete and passing**:
- All tests pass (existing + any new ones written)
- Linting passes
- CI checks pass
- The feature/fix actually works

If the Scout cannot achieve this, the Spec must document *why*.

### Spec Artifact Structure

```markdown
## Spec: [Issue Title]

### Summary
One paragraph describing the change and why it's needed.

### Implementation Approach
- What files need to change and why
- Key design decisions made during implementation
- Architecture/patterns used

### Discovered Pitfalls
- Edge cases found during implementation
- Non-obvious dependencies
- Things that looked simple but weren't

### Blockers & Dependencies  
- Other issues that should be completed first
- External dependencies discovered
- Questions that need human input (if any)

### Test Strategy
- What was tested during exploration
- Recommended test approach for final implementation

### Estimated Complexity
- Simple / Medium / Complex
- Rough scope: "~50 lines across 2 files" or "new module + integration"

### Files Touched (Reference)
- List of files modified in throwaway implementation
- NOT the code itself — just the map

### Scout Notes
- Anything else the Builder should know
- "I tried X and it didn't work because Y"
```

### Parallelism Model

- N Scouts can work simultaneously on N different issues
- No two Scouts work the same issue
- Scouts operate in complete isolation — throwaway branches never merge
- **No conflict possible because nothing persists**

---

## Spec Queue (Convergent Point)

### Queue Entry

```rust
struct SpecQueueEntry {
    id: String,
    issue_id: String,
    spec_content: String,
    scout_session_id: String,
    complexity: Complexity,
    dependencies: Vec<String>,
    queued_at: DateTime,
    status: SpecQueueStatus,
}

enum SpecQueueStatus {
    Pending,           // Awaiting review
    Approved,          // Ready for Builder
    NeedsRevision,     // Orchestrator requested changes
    Blocked,           // Dependencies not met
    Rejected,          // Needs re-exploration
}
```

### Prioritization

1. Dependencies resolved — Specs whose dependencies are all merged
2. Explicit priority — From issue labels/priority field
3. Complexity — Simpler specs first (configurable)
4. Age — FIFO within priority bands

### Orchestrator Review

Before approval, orchestrator checks:
- Is the Spec complete enough for a Builder?
- Are pitfalls documented?
- Are dependencies identified?
- Does the approach make architectural sense?

---

## Diamond 2: Implementation Phase

### Builder Workflow

1. Claim next approved Spec from Spec Queue
2. Receive context bundle:
   - The Spec
   - List of in-flight implementations
   - Recent merged changes
   - Pending Specs (what's coming next)
3. Create implementation branch (`impl/<issue>-<short-desc>`)
4. Implement from Spec
5. Verify: tests pass, lint passes, CI passes
6. Create PR with reference to Spec
7. PR enters Change Queue

### Context Bundle

```rust
struct BuilderContext {
    spec: SpecQueueEntry,
    in_flight: Vec<InFlightWork>,
    recent_merges: Vec<MergedPR>,
    upcoming_specs: Vec<SpecSummary>,
    main_sha: String,
}
```

### Serial Execution

**Only one Builder runs at a time.**

Why:
- Each implementation integrates with a known, stable `main`
- No merge conflicts between concurrent implementations
- Builder has full context of what just merged
- Predictable, debuggable state

---

## Change Queue (Merge Phase)

### Processing

1. Wait for CI to complete
2. Check mergeable status
   - Clean: proceed
   - Conflict: attempt auto-resolution or route back
3. Orchestrator final review (optional in Play mode)
4. Merge to main
5. Delete implementation branch
6. Close issue
7. Update context for any in-flight Builder

### Serial Merge

PRs merge one at a time, in queue order. After each merge, `main` advances and pending PRs rebase.

---

## Feedback Loops

| Scenario | Where Detected | Where It Goes Back |
|----------|---------------|-------------------|
| Spec incomplete/wrong | Orchestrator review | Re-exploration (new Scout) |
| Spec needs minor revision | Orchestrator review | Same/new Scout revises |
| Builder can't implement | Diamond 2 | Re-exploration with notes |
| CI fails on PR | Change Queue | Builder fixes |
| Merge conflict (trivial) | Change Queue | Auto-resolve + re-run CI |
| Merge conflict (non-trivial) | Change Queue | Builder re-implements |
| Human requests changes | Change Queue | Builder or Re-explore |

### Rejection Routing

```rust
enum RejectionRoute {
    BuilderFix { feedback: String },      // Minor — Builder can fix
    ReExplore { reason: String },         // Spec was wrong
    IssueNeedsRevision { feedback: String }, // Problem with issue itself
    Cancel { reason: String },            // Don't do this
}
```

---

## Key Differences from Current System

| Aspect | Current | Double Diamond |
|--------|---------|----------------|
| Parallel work | N agents implement parallel | N Scouts explore parallel, 1 Builder serial |
| Artifacts | Code persists, PRs created | Scouts: throwaway, only Spec persists |
| Conflict handling | Reactive | Proactive — serial prevents conflicts |
| Context sharing | None | Builder has full context |
| Knowledge capture | Lost on rejection | Spec preserves learnings |
| Failure mode | Wasted implementation | Wasted exploration (cheaper) |

---

## Open Questions

### Spec Format & Storage

1. Where does the Spec live? (GitHub comment, internal DB, both?)
2. Spec versioning — keep history or replace?

### Scout Lifecycle

3. Scout branch cleanup timing — immediate or keep until Spec approved?
4. Scout session reuse for revisions?
5. Scout failure handling — partial Spec, route to human, or retry?

### Builder Constraints

6. Builder timeout? (Current: 2hr)
7. Builder stuck protocol — ask Orchestrator? Fail? Ask human?
8. Fast-path for trivially simple changes?

### Queue Management

9. Max Spec Queue size?
10. Spec staleness — re-exploration trigger if main changes significantly?
11. Priority changes while in queue?

### Orchestrator Role

12. Orchestrator Spec review depth?
13. Can orchestrator Scout/Build directly for small tasks?

### Feedback Routing

14. Who decides rejection routing?
15. How much previous-attempt context does re-exploration Scout see?

### Human Interaction

16. Human injection points? (Write Specs, approve/reject, override ordering?)
17. Skip exploration for detailed human-authored issues?

### Metrics

18. Key metrics? (Exploration success rate, spec-to-merge rate, re-exploration rate, time-in-phase)

---

## Next Steps

1. Resolve critical open questions (especially #1, #7, #8, #14)
2. Design data model changes (SpecQueue, Scout/Builder task types)
3. Design prompt templates for Scout and Builder agents
4. Implement in phases:
   - Phase 1: Scout workflow + Spec artifact
   - Phase 2: Spec Queue + orchestrator review
   - Phase 3: Builder workflow + context bundle
   - Phase 4: Feedback loops

title: Add the ability to fire off individual tasks
body: Add a right click option or play button on a single task to fire it off - even if the cap is reached. It might need to pause or stop another task, which is fine.

title: v2 orchestrator: persistent Claude Code session driving the loop (plan steps 8+10)
body:
The orchestrator for v2: an MCP tool server over the Tasks store (plan step 8) plus a persistent headless Claude Code session (step 10) that reviews specs, ranks the queue, dispatches scouts, and routes feedback — event-driven, not interval-polled. See docs/plans/2026-04-17-v2-diamond-1.md §Orchestrator and docs/plans/2026-08-09-v2-resume.md.

Consolidates the v1-era orchestrator ideas, which remain good inputs:
- #530 proactive stream-of-consciousness chat
- #531 fire off investigation agents on review concerns
- #532 triage/decomposition of natural language into issues
- #534 autonomous behavior while the human is away
- #535 diagnose failures, suggest recovery
- #537 manage priority and dispatch ordering
- #538 post-merge reflection loop

title: Golden JSON wire fixtures shared by the Rust API and Swift client tests
body:
## Problem

The Swift app (`app/Tasks/Models.swift`) hand-maintains Codable models mirroring the Rust API types in `crates/tasks/src/models.rs` + `events.rs`. Nothing catches drift: a renamed field or new enum variant on the Rust side surfaces as a silent decode failure in the app. The agreed long-run approach (docs/clients.md § "Contract drift") is golden JSON fixtures both sides test against — not OpenAPI codegen yet.

## What to build

- A committed `fixtures/` directory (location: explore; suggest `crates/tasks/fixtures/` or repo-root `fixtures/`) containing one JSON file per wire shape: each entity (Project, Task, Session, Spec, SpecQueueItem, ModeResponse, error body) and one file per `EventPayload` variant wrapped in the `Event` envelope. Values should be deterministic (fixed timestamps/ids).
- A Rust test that serializes constructed instances and asserts byte-for-byte (or value-equal) match against the fixtures — failing with a helpful diff when a change is intentional, so updating a fixture is a conscious act.
- A Swift test target in `app/` that decodes every fixture through the app's real `JSONDecoder` configuration (see `TasksClient.makeDecoder()`); include coverage of the RFC3339 fractional-seconds variants chrono emits (0 and >3 digits).

Cover all snake_case enum string values (task states, session statuses, spec-queue statuses, mode, complexity) so an added variant forces a fixture update both sides see.

## Design decisions already made (do not revisit)

- Fixtures are the contract; neither side generates code from the other.
- Swift parsing stays lenient for *unknown* enum values at runtime (forward compatibility) — the fixtures test known values, they don't make parsing strict.

## Acceptance criteria

- `cargo test` fails if a Rust wire shape changes without a fixture update; the Swift test suite fails if the app can't decode a current fixture. A doc note in docs/clients.md pointing at the fixtures.
